characters: A cheerful child in a school uniform, pointing to eyes, ears, hands, legs, mouth, nose and chest in turn.

narrationPlan.voice: Bright, playful voice; children point as they hear each body part
narrationPlan.pace: Steady, with a pause for each action (about 70 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: A bright clapping beat with a simple tune of four notes (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Body-part action rhymes are common in nurseries everywhere. This one is original. Teachers can add the Twi, Ga, Ewe or other home-language words for body parts.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Check that every body part is named correctly and that the heart line is simple and true.

teacherGuide.overview: An action rhyme for naming body parts, counting one and two, and learning to care for the body. Form: five couplets. Rhyming pairs: see/me, clap/tap, say/day, smell/well, right/night.
learningGoals: Name three ways to care for the body.
beforeReading: Play a game: touch your nose, touch your ears, touch your knees.
whileReading: Point to each part as it is named. Slow down so everyone can follow.
afterReading: Ask: which body parts do we wash every day?
Draw a body and label two parts.
discussion: How do we look after our eyes and ears?
reflection: What is one way you looked after your body today?

mathsExtension.task: How many eyes and ears do you have together?

support: Say one line at a time and let children echo and point.
stretch: Add a verse about two feet, ten toes and one tongue.

culturalNotes: Body-part action rhymes are common in nurseries everywhere. This one is original. Teachers can add the Twi, Ga, Ewe or other home-language words for body parts.
localiseThis: Invite children to say the body words in their home language.
